analysis.one_liner: Requires upfront all-in pricing for hotel, ticket, and internet bills, bans most early-termination fees, and stops airlines charging for kids' family seating.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: it sat in two House committees and its subcommittees until the 118th Congress ended, so no junk fee ban became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The Junk Fee Prevention Act would require businesses that sell short-term lodging or event tickets to show the full price, including all mandatory fees, in every ad and at checkout [S2]. It would ban excessive or deceptive mandatory fees, bar most early-termination fees on internet, mobile, and pay-TV service, and require airlines to seat children 13 and under next to a parent at no extra charge [S2, S3]. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the pricing rules, and the Federal Communications Commission the communications rules [S2, S3]. The bill was referred to two House committees in April 2023 and received no further action before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who book hotels and vacation rentals, buy event tickets, subscribe to internet/mobile/pay-TV, or fly with young children. They would see the real price up front instead of fees added at checkout, could not be charged for ending a service contract early, and would not pay extra for their child to sit next to them on a plane. State attorneys general gain new power to sue for refunds on residents' behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers buying lodging, tickets, phone/internet service, flights

how_it_helps.text: Businesses selling short-term lodging or event tickets must show the full price, including all mandatory fees, in every ad and at the first price display, and the price cannot change during checkout.

Ticket sellers must disclose refund and guarantee policies before purchase, reveal how many tickets are actually available for sale before public presales, and warn buyers and offer refunds when they do not possess the ticket at the time of sale.
Internet, mobile, and pay-TV providers can no longer charge excessive or unreasonable early-termination fees, and the FCC must consider forcing disclosure of or banning other hidden mandatory fees.
Airlines must seat each child 13 or younger next to an accompanying adult at no extra charge, or offer rebooking, a full refund, or other alternatives.
The FTC and state attorneys general can enforce the pricing rules, giving states the power to sue for refunds and restitution on behalf of residents.

analysis.who_pays: Ticketing companies, short-term lodging platforms, internet/mobile/pay-TV providers, and airlines, which would lose fee revenue and face FTC, FCC, and state enforcement. Airlines specifically would lose fees for family seating. Some compliance cost to restructure advertised pricing.

drawbacks.text: The bill's ban on fees that are 'excessive or deceptive' delegates to the FTC and FCC, through rulemaking and court judgments, the judgment of when a fee is out of proportion to the cost of the service provided — a standard businesses and judges could contest for years, creating legal uncertainty.

Requiring total prices (including all mandatory fees) in every advertisement could make some ads longer or more complex, and firms might restructure fees rather than lower them, though the bill bans fees that are not reasonably avoidable or that a reasonable consumer would expect to be included.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are direct and broad — honest pricing, fewer surprise charges, no family-seating fees, and real enforcement tools — while the costs fall on companies that profit from hidden fees and on consumers in the form of less itemized advertising. The main design risk is that the FTC's open-ended authority to police "excessive" fees could be broad or inconsistently applied, but that is a modest cost against a meaningful consumer protection. The bill died without a committee hearing or vote, so its costs and benefits never got a real test in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees, which sent it to subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 3, 2023, and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees.
In its first two days it was sent to the Aviation and the Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittees — the last recorded action on the bill.
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines, ticketing platforms, lodging operators, and telecom companies keep charging the hidden fees the bill would have restricted; consumers keep paying them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, ticket sellers, lodging and telecom firms

against.what_they_did: Received the referral but never reported the bill or scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were House Democrats [S4], and no committee or floor action ever occurred, so the record shows no Republican position on the bill itself; junk fee rules were being advanced separately by the FTC under the administration's broader fee-crackdown push (widely reported).

industries.note: They must advertise all-in prices, disclose inventory before presales, and warn buyers when they do not hold the ticket. These fees and holdbacks are significant revenue, and consumers currently pay them at checkout.
Cleaning and 'resort' fees tacked on at checkout must be folded into the advertised price, ending the gap between the listed rate and the bill.
Early-termination fees are banned and the FCC must consider banning or forcing disclosure of other mandatory fees, cutting into revenue streams many consumers experience as billing surprises.
They lose the ability to charge families extra for adjacent child seating, a fee stream the bill outright prohibits.
